title: Veridian Systems - dedicated warm-pool & burst play discovery
transcript_header: 2027-11-03 14:00 PT | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Samir Kaur, Ivy Chen - Redwood; Marcelo Ruiz, Aisha Patel, Tom Hargreaves - Veridian Systems
summary: Intro discovery to map Veridian's inference needs. Customer runs multi-tenant LLM features with spiky traffic; primary asks: reserved GPUs for predictable latency, tenant isolation, warm-pool / prewarm strategy for burst, and compliance (SSO, KMS, audit logs). Redwood AE+SE covered Dedicated model variants, warm-pool sizing, fallback and cost/latency tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: pricing + prewarm calc, SOC2 + network diagram, schedule 1-week pilot and loadbench window.
topics: Fallbacks to hosted variants and graceful degradation

transcript: 00:00:00 - Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about 45 minutes on the calendar, will do a quick intro then ivy will dig into architecture, sound good?
00:00:12 - Marcelo (Veridian): yep, thanks Samir, appreciate it. We pulled in aisha and tom, we'll try to keep it focused around the surge scenario and security needs.

00:00:35 - Ivy (Redwood SE): thanks, quick intro from us — i’m ivy, i handle deployments and dedicated infra. we typically talk through traffic patterns, isolation, and prewarm options — and then sizing. any constraints we should know up-front?

00:00:48 - Tom (Veridian/CTO): the big ones are: P1 latency < 250ms tail, data residency for EU users, and strict tenant isolation for some regulated customers. also we want cost predictability — bursts are big but short, like 10x baseline for 2-5 minutes
00:01:05 - Marcelo: yeah our notification flows spike a lot — we have a mix of batch embeddings and realtime chat completions, the chat ones are the SLO-sensitive bit.
00:01:30 - Samir: got it. can you share a rough shape of those spikes? average qps and tail?

00:01:45 - Marcelo: our 95th is usually fine but we see 99.9 at 800ms during campaigns. avg qps for chat is ~30 rps, peak goes to 300 for 3-7 minutes. embeddings are heavy throughput but tolerant of 1s lat. i'll get a csv out.

00:02:20 - Ivy: that maps well to dedicated pools with a warm-pool prewarm strategy. conceptually you reserve node capacity (dedicated) and keep a warm pool of model instances prewarmed. when spikes hit we instant-fork, or route to warm nodes to hit the tail SLO. there are a few knobs: pool size, prewarm per GPU, prewarmed sequence length, and kv cache priming.
00:03:05 - Aisha (Platform Eng): can you explain kv cache priming? our ops team calls it K V cash sometimes, sorry —

00:03:16 - Ivy: yeah totally — KV cache priming means keeping the model's past key-value cache populated to avoid initial slow token generation. if you have repeating prompts or rooted contexts you can prime. it reduces first-token latency for long context models.
00:03:45 - Tom: how does that interact with multi-tenant isolation? we can't have one customer's context leaking into another's warm instance.

00:03:58 - Ivy: right — two isolation patterns: strict tenant fencing: dedicate nodes per tenant (or per tenant group) so KV cache never crosses tenants; soft fencing: shared pool with per-request context scrubbers and per-tenant KV namespace. soft fencing is more cost-efficient but stricter compliance customers usually insist on dedicated tenancy.
00:04:30 - Marcelo: for our regulated verticals we need node-level separation, the rest could be shared. curious what Redwood's warm-pool billing looks like — are we billed for prewarmed GPU time?

00:04:50 - Samir: yes for Dedicated reserved GPUs you're committing capacity. warm instances on those GPUs count toward utilization; we show a breakdown in the pricing sheet — there's also burst credits / transient burst options for short overage. we can model a hybrid: reserved pool for critical tenants + shared warm pool for general traffic, with auto-fallback to hosted variants if capacity exhausted.
00:05:25 - Aisha: hosted fallback — wouldn't that hit data residency issues if EU data goes to hosted us region?

00:05:35 - Ivy: good call. fallback routing is policy-driven — you can restrict fallbacks by region or by customer tag; in your case we'd fallback to a smaller model within the same region or to another dedicated pool in eu if you have multi-region dedicated capacity.
00:06:05 - Tom: can Redwood guarantee the prewarm state is preserved across node reboots? we've had evictions in our k8s clusters that clear cache and kill tails.

00:06:18 - Ivy: Dedicated instances are managed by our runtime and we persist model KV where possible; warm-pool prewarmed runners are kept hot and not scheduled away. in the extremely rare case of host failure, we have a fast cold start path and can route to a smaller lower-latency model variant while the warm pool recovers — that's part of the graceful degradation story.
00:06:45 - Marcelo: what's the typical cold start hit? like 2-3 seconds?

00:06:52 - Ivy: depends on model & quantization. For a 30B fp16 model cold start might be 1.5-3s, int8 quantized could be 0.6-1.2s. our prewarm reduces that to sub-200-300ms first token in many cases.

00:07:20 - Samir: and the cost tradeoff we usually show: more warm capacity increases steady cost but reduces tail latency and reduces user-perceived errors. we can run cost modeling for your 30->300 rps spikes.
00:07:40 - Aisha: curious about autoscaling — we need predictable behavior during bursts. does Redwood do immediate scale-up or use queued requests?

00:07:50 - Ivy: Dedicated supports a combination: instant warm-pool routing for sub-second responses; autoscale to spin more runners if burst sustains beyond a threshold. we also have a queuing/circuit-breaker policy for backpressure to maintain SLOs for priority tenants.
00:08:12 - Tom: any tenant-level rate limiting and RBAC? compliance teams need RBAC for API keys and audit logs.
00:08:22 - Samir: yes, Redwood Console supports token-level RBAC, SSO/SAML, and audit trails. we integrate with customer KMS for keying, and we can show SOC2 artifacts — we'll attach those docs.
00:08:45 - Marcelo: perfect, that helps. Are there specific prewarm heuristics you recommend for chat vs embeddings?

00:08:55 - Ivy: chat needs many small, low-latency workers; keep warm instances sized for expected concurrency per GPU. embeddings are better batched — you can run larger batch workers with longer lat tolerances. for chat we often prewarm 8-16 model instances per GPU depending on model and latency requirement.
00:09:20 - Aisha: 8-16 seems high, our baseline is 30 rps, peak 300. what numbers would you plug in?

00:09:30 - Ivy: as a rough example: for a 30B model on an A100-style GPU, 12 warm copies can sustain ~120-150 concurrent chat tokens-per-second with sub-200ms tail, but exacts depend on input length; we'll run a sim given your telemetry and return concrete numbers.
00:10:00 - Speaker 1: (background noise) —
00:10:12 - Marcelo: one more — we want an autoscale safety buffer but also a cost cap. is there a way to cold-start to a smaller model automatically when cost threshold hit?

00:10:25 - Ivy: yes, policy-driven model routing: route to a lower-cost quantized variant or smaller arch. you can set cost thresholds per route so after a percentile of spend we fallback to cheaper model. Redwood Optimize can recommend which quantized variant has acceptable quality drop for your prompts.
00:11:00 - Tom: how do you measure quality drop? we need to avoid regressions for some flows (billing/legal text).

00:11:10 - Samir: we link rollouts to eval sets — you can run A/B with canaries, Redwood will track regressions on your prompt suites and alert. for legal/billing you can pin to the full model or set stricter rollback thresholds.
00:11:35 - Aisha: network egress — we have strict egress policies, will Redwood need open egress to vendor endpoints?

00:11:45 - Ivy: for Private deployment you control egress. For Dedicated we can operate VPC peered deployments or private endpoints. We'll need a handful of control-plane endpoints for management, but data plane can remain in-customer region with VPC-only routing.
00:12:10 - Marcelo: ok. curious about warm-pool warm-up costs — if we prewarm 12 instances per GPU for 3 reserved GPUs, are we billed as 36 instance-hours?

00:12:25 - Samir: yes effectively you're paying for reserved GPU capacity; the warm runners occupy that capacity. Our pricing sheet will show per-GPU monthly cost and an example amortization for warm instances. we also offer a burst buffer for short overages billed separately to avoid long term commit for brief campaigns.
00:12:50 - Aisha: what's the burst buffer mechanics? is it shared across customers?

00:12:58 - Ivy: burst buffer is a cross-tenant capacity pool within a region for Redwood-managed overflow; you can choose to opt-in or keep all traffic within your dedicated pools. for compliance-sensitive tenants you would opt out.
00:13:20 - Tom: can we do per-tenant prewarm caps so critical tenants always get warm instances?
00:13:28 - Ivy: yes, priority routing / static reservations per tenant are supported. that's the node-level separation we mentioned earlier.
00:13:40 - Marcelo: let's talk pilot: we'd like a 1-week pilot simulating our worst-case campaign. can Redwood run loadbench with us?
00:13:50 - Samir: absolutely — typical pilot is 1 week with a dedicated pool and a load window. we'll coordinate the loadbench scripts and have Ivy observe metrics and tune warm-pool sizing.
00:14:10 - Aisha: in terms of observability, do we get token-level latency and cost breakdowns per route?
00:14:20 - Ivy: yes Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-model/per-route latency heatmaps, and traces. you can also export to your telemetry stack.
00:14:45 - Speaker 2 (background): hmm —
00:15:02 - Marcelo: security artifacts — please send SOC2, ISO42 something? (laughter) — I'm kidding but yes ISO/ SOC 2 reports would be important
00:15:12 - Samir: we'll attach SOC2 Type II and our data handling whitepaper; for Private we have an on-prem package too.
00:15:28 - Aisha: one more technical nit — how are model updates/rollouts handled to avoid warm-pool eviction or mismatch? We don't want differences across replicas mid-traffic.

00:15:40 - Ivy: rollouts are versioned. We support canary traffic, A/B, and automatic rollback. warm-pool instances are labelled by version, and we drain and replace pools in a controlled fashion to keep consistency. you can pin tenants to specific model versions during rollout.
00:16:05 - Tom: do you support bring-your-own models? we have an internal fine-tuned model we want to serve privately.
00:16:13 - Ivy: yes BYOM is supported on Dedicated and Private. we'll need the model artifacts and some tests — we can advise quantization profiles to reduce memory footprint.
00:16:30 - Marcelo: great. can you also comment on metrics for warm-to-cold transitions? we care about tail percentiles during the first 60 seconds of an unexpected spike.
00:16:40 - Ivy: we capture first-token latency percentiles and have instrumentation for warm-hit rates. for your pilot we can generate a heatmap of warm-hit vs cold-hit over the load window.

00:17:05 - Samir: ok wrap up — i'll send pricing and the prewarm calculator. ivy will send the warm-pool sizing doc and a short PDF on KV cache priming. you (marcelo) will send telemetry and aisha will send the network diagram. we'll propose pilot dates in the follow-up.
00:17:25 - Marcelo: sounds good. one question — do you have any references of similar customers with high burst patterns?
00:17:33 - Samir: yes i can share anonymized case studies — i'll ping two references who ran 10x+ spikes with dedicated warm pools. i'll include links in the email.
00:17:50 - Aisha: thanks, also send us details about the control-plane endpoints so our security team can vet egress rules.
00:18:00 - Samir: will do. any last-minute items?
00:18:05 - Tom: nope that's it from me. thanks everyone.
00:18:12 - Ivy: thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and a proposed pilot plan. bye.
00:18:20 - End of recording
